comments.text:
The Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871 (also known as the Civil Rights Act of 1871) was a landmark federal law passed to combat white supremacist terrorism during the Reconstruction era. It empowered the federal government to protect the constitutional rights of African Americans when state governments failed to do so.
​Key Provisions
​Federal Intervention: It authorized the President to use military force to suppress insurgencies and domestic violence.
​Habeas Corpus: It gave the President the authority to suspend the writ of habeas corpus to hold prisoners without immediate charges.
​Civil Liability (Section 1983): It established the right for individuals to sue state officials in federal court for civil rights violations, a provision still widely used today.
​Anti-Conspiracy: It made it a federal crime for individuals to conspire to deprive others of "equal protection of the laws."
​Impact
​President Ulysses S. Grant used the act to declare martial law in nine South Carolina counties, leading to thousands of arrests that effectively dismantled the first iteration of the KKK. While the Act fell into disuse after Reconstruction ended in 1877, its core legal mechanisms were revived during the 1960s Civil Rights Movement and remain central to modern civil rights litigation.
